summary: This informational RFC reserves multicast addresses for use in documentation and examples, and explains how addresses derived from AS numbers or unicast addresses can be used that way too.

plainLanguage.summary: Books use fake phone numbers in examples so nobody real gets called. This sets aside fake group addresses for examples.

how do i derive glop addresses for documentation
subtitle: Reserved multicast addresses and schemes for use in documentation and examples.

tldr.problem: Documentation and examples can accidentally use real multicast addresses, creating a risk that example code impacts production networks.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC reserves specific multicast address blocks for documentation and explains how to derive example addresses from reserved unicast prefixes and AS numbers.
tldr.outcome: Writers and instructors can safely use 233.252.0.0/24 for IPv4 and FF0X::DB8:0:0/96 for IPv6 in examples without risk.

today: RFC 6676 is an Informational Internet Standard and has not been obsoleted. It is the canonical reference for multicast documentation addresses.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
When writing technical documentation and IETF specifications, examples often need to include multicast addresses. Without reserved addresses for this purpose, example code could accidentally send traffic to real multicast groups in use on production networks. This RFC reserves specific multicast address ranges for documentation only, similar to how RFC 5737 reserves unicast addresses like 192.0.2.0/24 and RFC 3849 reserves 2001:DB8::/32 for documentation.

The document defines both direct address reservations and guidance on deriving documentation addresses from reserved unicast prefixes and AS numbers, so that examples can use consistent addressing schemes without risk.
sections.plainLanguage: Just like books print fake phone numbers starting with 555 so real people don't get random calls, this RFC picks special network addresses that documentation can use without accidentally affecting real networks.

sections.title: IPv4 Documentation Multicast Addresses
sections.content:
For IPv4, the reserved multicast addresses for documentation are 233.252.0.0/24. This block is reserved for Any-Source Multicast (ASM) examples, where any source can send to the group.

For Source-Specific Multicast (SSM) examples, writers should use the documentation unicast addresses from RFC 5737 (192.0.2.0/24, 198.51.100.0/24, and 203.0.113.0/24) as the source addresses. The RFC also provides guidance on deriving addresses using two additional methods: Administratively Scoped multicast addresses (using offset 10 within reserved scopes) and GLOP addresses derived from the reserved AS numbers 64496–64511, which produce the prefixes 233.251.240.0/24 through 233.251.255.0/24.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv4 has one block of fake multicast addresses (233.252.0.0/24) that's always safe to use in examples. For other methods, you can build them from the fake unicast addresses or fake AS numbers reserved for documentation.

sections.title: IPv6 Documentation Multicast Addresses
sections.content:
For IPv6, the reserved multicast addresses for documentation are FF0X::DB8:0:0/96. This is a /96 prefix that allows use with different scope values (represented by the X). The addresses are marked as permanently assigned (T-flag is zero), making them suitable for stable documentation examples.

For Source-Specific Multicast (SSM) examples, writers should use the reserved IPv6 unicast prefix 2001:DB8::/32 as the source addresses. The RFC explains how to derive Unicast Prefix-Based IPv6 multicast addresses from this documentation prefix and how to create Embedded-RP addresses where the Rendezvous Point IPv6 address is embedded inside the multicast group address.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv6 has a similar block of fake multicast addresses (starting with FF0X::DB8) for documentation. You can also build examples using the fake IPv6 address prefix 2001:DB8, which is well known as a documentation placeholder.

sections.title: Deployment and Operational Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC recommends that network operators filter out multicast traffic destined to these documentation addresses to further reduce any risk of accidental impact. Tools that process multicast signalling can also be configured to filter and discard signalling packets for these reserved addresses. This defense-in-depth approach ensures that even if example code escapes into production, these addresses will not be assigned or used by actual services.

The use of these reserved addresses has no negative impact on network security; instead, the practice improves operational safety by preventing documentation examples from interfering with real multicast traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: Networks can also filter out these fake addresses at the borders, so even if example code somehow runs on a real network, the fake addresses won't cause problems.
